pages.subtitle: A woman took a host for a wrong reason, and a light shining in the night led her to say she was sorry.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A stolen host was reported to bleed and to shine with light

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Shrine of the Holy Miracle (Church of Saint Stephen) in Santarém

pages.intro: In the 1200s, in the town of Santarém, Portugal, a woman took a consecrated host from church to use in a spell. That was a very wrong thing to do. According to tradition, the host began to bleed, and that night a bright light shone from where she had hidden it. She told the truth, and the host was carried back to church, where it is still honored today.
story_paragraphs: Long ago, in the town of Santarém, Portugal, there lived a woman who was unhappy in her marriage. She was jealous and wanted her husband to love her more.

She went to a sorceress, a woman who claimed to do magic. The sorceress told her to bring back a consecrated host from church to use in a spell. Using the Body of Jesus for magic is a terrible wrong, but the woman did it anyway. At Mass, she received the host but did not consume it. She wrapped it in a cloth and hurried away.
According to the story, the host began to bleed, and the cloth was stained. Frightened, the woman hid the host in a drawer in her bedroom.
That night, a bright light shone from the drawer and filled the room. Her husband saw the light and asked what was happening. The woman told him everything.

In the morning, they went to their parish priest. The priest came to their house, took the host, and carried it back in a procession to the Church of Saint Stephen. People came from all around to see it.

The host was placed in a container of beeswax. Years later, the story says, the wax container was found broken, and the blood was inside a crystal container instead. Church investigations in 1340 and 1612 studied the event.

Today, the relic is kept above the main altar of the Church of Saint Stephen, now called the Shrine of the Holy Miracle. The couple's house became a chapel. Every year, people carry the relic in a procession from the house to the church. The woman's story reminds us that it is never too late to tell the truth and turn back to God.

pages.subtitle: A host was found unharmed in a fire in 1345, and people in Amsterdam still walk in silent prayer to remember it.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A host was reported found unharmed in the ashes of a fire

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Silent Walk (Stille Omgang) through Amsterdam each March

pages.intro: In March 1345, a very sick man in Amsterdam received Holy Communion. He was too ill to keep the host down, and, as was the custom, it was put into the fire. The next morning, the host was found whole in the ashes. For centuries since, Catholics in Amsterdam have honored the miracle, and today they still walk through the city at night in silent prayer.
story_paragraphs: Amsterdam is a city in the Netherlands, known for its canals. In March 1345, a man who lived on a street called the Kalverstraat was very sick. He thought he was dying, so he asked for a priest to give him the last sacraments, including Holy Communion.

The priest came and gave him the host. But the man was so sick that he could not keep it down. The people caring for him did what was the custom at that time: they put what he could not keep down into the fire.
The next morning, according to the story, they found the host lying in the ashes. It was whole and unharmed. They were amazed.

A priest carried the host back to the parish church. But twice, the story says, the host was found back at the house on the Kalverstraat. So the people carried it in a solemn procession to the church, where it stayed.
A chapel was built where the house had stood. Amsterdam became a great place of pilgrimage, and every year people walked in procession to honor the miracle.

In 1578, the leaders of the city became Protestant and banned Catholic services and processions. But Catholics did not forget. They kept praying in hidden churches. Some walked the old procession route quietly, without singing or carrying anything, so no one could stop them.

That quiet walk became the Stille Omgang, which means "Silent Walk." Today, every March, thousands of Catholics walk through the streets of Amsterdam at night in silence, praying. They remember the miracle and pray for their city and their faith.

pages.subtitle: In 1608, a fire burned the altar of an abbey church, but the monstrance holding the Eucharist was found hanging in the air.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A monstrance was reported to hang in the air after a fire, for 33 hours

pages.intro: In 1608, at a monastery in Faverney, France, the Eucharist was displayed on the altar for people to pray before it at Pentecost. During the night, a fire burned the altar. When the monks came in, they found the monstrance, the holder for the Eucharist, hanging in the air above the ashes. According to the reports, it stayed there for 33 hours while thousands watched.
story_paragraphs: Faverney is a small town in the east of France. In 1608, monks lived there in an abbey, a large monastery with a church.

On the eve of Pentecost, the monks placed the Eucharist on a special altar in the church so that people could come and pray before it. The host was in a monstrance, a beautiful holder that lets people see the Eucharist. Candles were lit all around it.
During the night, while the church was empty, a fire broke out. It burned the altar and everything on it, including the cloths and decorations.
In the morning, the monks rushed in. To their amazement, the monstrance had not burned. It was hanging in the air, with nothing holding it up, above the ruins of the altar.

News spread quickly. People came from the town and the villages around to see. According to the reports, the monstrance stayed in the air for about 33 hours, and thousands of people saw it. Then, during a Mass, it came gently down onto a new altar.
The Church leaders of the area studied what had happened. They spoke with many witnesses and wrote down what they said.

One of the hosts from the monstrance is still kept at Faverney today. In 2008, for the 400th anniversary of the miracle, more than 7,000 people came to Faverney to pray. The cardinal who preached that day said, "It is not a hoax, it is a wonder." He reminded people that the most important miracle happens at every Mass, when Jesus comes to us in the Eucharist.

pages.subtitle: In 1453, a soldier stole a monstrance, and in the city square the Eucharist rose into the air.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: A stolen host was reported to rise into the air and shine

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Basilica of Corpus Domini in Turin

pages.intro: In 1453, during a war in the mountains of northern Italy, a soldier stole a monstrance holding the Eucharist from a village church. He carried it to the city of Turin on a mule. In the city square, the mule stumbled. According to the story, the Eucharist rose high into the air, shining, until the bishop came and it came down into his chalice.
story_paragraphs: In 1453, there was fighting in the mountain valleys west of Turin, in northern Italy. Soldiers came into the village of Exilles and robbed its church.

One soldier broke open the tabernacle. Inside was a monstrance, a beautiful holder for the Eucharist, with a consecrated host in it. The soldier stuffed it into a sack with other stolen things, loaded it onto a mule, and set off for the city of Turin to sell what he had taken.
On June 6, 1453, the soldier and his mule came into the main square of Turin, near the church of Saint Sylvester. Suddenly, the mule stumbled and fell. The sack fell open.

According to the story, the monstrance rose up out of the sack, high above the houses around the square. People stopped and stared. Then the monstrance came down, but the host stayed in the air, shining like the sun.

Someone ran to tell the bishop of Turin, Ludovico of Romagnano. He hurried to the square with priests and people. The bishop knelt and prayed. Then he held up a chalice, and the host came gently down into it.

The people carried the host into the cathedral with great joy. At the place where the mule fell, they first built a small shrine. Later, a beautiful church was built there. It is called Corpus Domini, which means "the Body of the Lord."

In 1853, for the 400th anniversary, Pope Pius IX approved a special Mass for Turin to celebrate the miracle. The host of 1453 is no longer kept, but people still pray at the place in the square where the miracle is remembered.

pages.student_title: The Eucharistic Miracle of O Cebreiro
pages.subtitle: A farmer walked through a snowstorm to get to Mass, and a priest who doubted saw something he never forgot.

quick_facts.label: What happened
quick_facts.value: The bread and wine were reported to change into flesh and blood

quick_facts.label: Remembered at
quick_facts.value: The Church of Santa María la Real in O Cebreiro

pages.intro: High in the mountains of northern Spain is a tiny village called O Cebreiro. About the year 1300, according to tradition, a farmer walked through a terrible snowstorm to get to Mass. The priest thought he was foolish to come so far for a little bread and wine. But at the consecration, the story says, the bread and wine changed to look like real flesh and blood.
story_paragraphs: O Cebreiro is a little village high on a mountain in Galicia, in the northwest of Spain. It sits on the Camino de Santiago, the old pilgrim road to the tomb of Saint James. Long ago, monks there cared for the pilgrims who passed by.

About the year 1300, a monk there was celebrating Mass on a cold winter day. He had lost much of his faith. He said Mass out of habit, without really believing that Jesus becomes present in the Eucharist.
That day, a great snowstorm was blowing. No one was expected at Mass. But a farmer named Juan Santín, from the nearby village of Barxamaior, had walked through the deep snow and wind to be there.
When the priest saw him, he scoffed. He thought the farmer was foolish to risk so much just for "a bit of bread and wine."

Then the priest said the words of consecration. According to the story, the host in his hands changed and looked like real flesh. The wine in the chalice became blood, and it spilled onto the altar cloth. The priest was amazed and ashamed. Juan Santín's strong faith had been rewarded, and the priest's doubt was turned to faith.

The chalice and paten from that Mass are still kept at O Cebreiro. In 1486, Queen Isabella of Spain gave a silver reliquary to hold the relics. The next year, in 1487, Pope Innocent VIII recognized the miracle.
Today, people walking the Camino de Santiago stop at the old stone church of Santa María la Real to pray. The chalice and host even appear on the coat of arms of Galicia.
